articles.title: Three children dead and a mistrial: What is the Lindsay Clancy case?
articles.summary: US News: The closely watched trial of Massachusetts mother Lindsay Clancy, accused of killing her three young children, ended in a mistrial on Friday after jur.
articles.body: The closely watched trial of Massachusetts mother Lindsay Clancy, accused of killing her three young children, ended in a mistrial on Friday after jurors failed to reach a verdict following seven days of deliberations. The dramatic conclusion came after a five-week trial that focused largely on one question: Was Clancy criminally responsible for the deaths, or was she suffering from severe mental illness at the time?Clancy, 36, has never disputed that she strangled her children: Cora, 5, Dawson, 3, and eight-month-old Callan, at the family’s home in Duxbury, Massachusetts, on January 24, 2023. Her defence argued that she was experiencing postpartum psychosis, suffering from hallucinations and delusions that left her unable to understand the nature of her actions. Prosecutors, however, argued that the killings were intentional and calculated and that Clancy knew what she was doing.What happened to Lindsay Clancy’s children?Prosecutors allege that on January 24, 2023, Clancy intentionally strangled all three of her children at their home south of Boston. After the killings, she jumped from a second-floor window in an apparent suicide attempt.Her husband, Patrick Clancy, had left the house to get food and medication. When he returned, he found the children dead in the basement and Clancy seriously injured outside the house. She suffered severe spinal injuries in the fall and was left paralysed from the waist down. She attended the trial in a wheelchair.Patrick described the last time he saw his son Dawson alive, recalling him sitting on the couch eating chicken nuggets before he left the house. When he returned, the children were dead.A recording of Patrick’s 911 call was played in court, with him screaming, "She killed the kids". Clancy sobbed as the recording was played.Clancy's family members testified that her mental health had deteriorated significantly in the weeks before the killings. Her former mother-in-law Susan Clancy said she was "begging for help", while her mother Paula Musgrove testified that Clancy had told her she was having thoughts of harming her children.Her sister Allison Ozga told the court that Clancy was experiencing suicidal thoughts every day in the month before the killings. Defence says postpartum psychosis led to killingsThe central issue at trial was not whether Clancy killed her children, but whether she was legally responsible for doing so.Her lawyers argued that she was suffering from postpartum psychosis, a rare and severe mental health condition that can involve hallucinations, delusions, mania and depression following childbirth. They pointed to her treatment for mental health problems and the fact that she had checked herself into a psychiatric hospital just days before the deaths.Clancy, a former labour and delivery nurse, had also sought help from a suicide hotline and an emergency room and was prescribed more than a dozen medications during her treatment.The defence presented evidence that Clancy had become increasingly paranoid, depressed and suicidal. Her family described her as a loving and nurturing mother who changed dramatically after the birth of her youngest child.Her husband said her "big spiral" began about a month before the children died."She started to lose a lot of weight, and she became very depressed, and she was having a really hard time," he said.But prosecutors presented a different picture. They argued that Clancy deliberately sent Patrick out on errands before killing the children and that her actions showed she understood what she was doing.More than 10 expert witnesses testified during the trial, with psychiatrists and other specialists offering conflicting views about Clancy’s mental state and whether the evidence supported a diagnosis of postpartum psychosis.One prosecution psychiatrist, Jennifer Tufts, testified that Clancy had not shown signs of psychosis during their sessions. She said there were "no serious signs that her safety or anyone else's safety was at risk".The defence challenged her testimony, pointing to medical notes that referred to Clancy's "not hyper, pressured speech". Tufts rejected the interpretation put forward by the defence, saying the "not" applied to both "hyper" and "pressured"."I don't care what it says. I know what I meant," she said. Trial ends in deadlock after courtroom dramaThe five-week trial attracted widespread attention, with thousands of people following the proceedings online. Hundreds of women also gathered outside the courthouse in support of Clancy, wearing pink shirts carrying messages including "She Needed Help" and "Peace For Lindsay".The trial itself was marked by several clashes between lawyers and witnesses.Two days before closing arguments, the defence sought a mistrial after prosecutors questioned witnesses about Clancy’s Catholic faith. The judge later instructed jurors to disregard the testimony, calling it an "absolutely inappropriate area of testimony"."It is to be stricken. It is not to be considered. I can't be any more clear of that," Judge William F. Sullivan said.The biggest drama, however, came during jury deliberations.After seven days, the jury remained deadlocked. A note from the jury indicated that one juror was allegedly not following the judge's instructions concerning reasonable doubt. Clancy's lawyer Kevin Reddington asked for the juror to be removed, but Sullivan rejected the request and instead instructed the jury again on the law.On Friday, Sullivan was preparing to declare a mistrial when Reddington made a last-minute appeal to Massachusetts' highest court, seeking to stop the declaration and have the disputed juror removed.The appeal was rejected, and Sullivan formally declared a mistrial.Reddington blamed the deadlock on the juror, saying the other jurors had been "robbed" of the chance to reach a verdict."They know they were robbed by one man, for whatever his agenda was, who stole seven weeks of the life of these other jurors that were so attentive, so beautiful, so wonderful," he said outside the courthouse. "You could see how defeated they were sitting there. I got a funny feeling they would have gone on for another week if they had to. So I hope that guy can sleep well at night."Prosecutors disputed the defence's characterisation of the juror, arguing there was nothing in the jury's notes showing "a lack of impartiality, bias, extraneous influence, or inability to deliberate." What happens to Lindsay Clancy after the mistrial?The mistrial does not amount to an acquittal, and Clancy remains charged with three counts of first-degree murder.Judge Sullivan has scheduled a hearing for September 29. The defence could ask him to declare Clancy not guilty, although such a move is considered unlikely to succeed.The prosecution could seek a second trial, negotiate a plea deal or, in theory, drop the case. Plymouth County District Attorney Timothy Cruz said there would be no immediate decision on whether to retry Clancy.But Cruz made clear that prosecutors continue to view the case as one involving three murdered children."This case was about Lindsay Clancy and what she did … the cruel and calculated killing of three innocents," Cruz said shortly after court ended on Friday. He later continued, "Children were murdered and it’s our job to seek justice."A retrial would mean another lengthy and emotionally difficult process for Clancy's family and for Patrick Clancy, who has already testified about the deaths of his children.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: 'Step beyond books to connect with children': PM Modi's message on Teachers' Day
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: Prime Minister Narendra Modi has urged teachers to “step beyond textbooks” to ensure that children do not lose out on their childhood.The p.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Prime Minister Narendra Modi has urged teachers to “step beyond textbooks” to ensure that children do not lose out on their childhood.The prime minister's message came during his interaction with recipients of the National Teachers’ Awards at his residence on Friday, a day ahead of Teachers’ Day, which commemorates the birth anniversary of former President and renowned educationist Dr Sarvepalli Radhakrishnan."We need to step outside of books and the syllabus much more than before and get into the lives of children. Childhood shouldn't be allowed to die. And the biggest task of keeping childhood alive can be done by a teacher. It's the teacher's job to ensure the child within remains," he said.To drive home his point, PM Modi cited growing screen addiction among children, particularly their increasing dependence on video games. He also flagged drug consumption as a concern, saying the problem was no longer confined to universities or major cities."Screen time has now become a form of addiction. A thought occurs to me: if a child begins to take a keen interest in sports, and by sports, I don't mean video games but actually playing on the field. Then slowly, they can come out of it. And we should make it a habit to involve kids as much as possible in creativity, and we should design some programmes for that," the prime minister said."Now take the case of drugs. It's not just in big cities or universities anymore, nobody even knows what it is; someone just comes and gives it. Teachers should watch for behavioural changes in children," he added.Saturday marks the 138th birth anniversary of Dr Sarvepalli Radhakrishnan, who also served as Vice President of India. articles.title: Bootle mum's CCTV catches footage of suspected arson attack at her home
articles.summary: Holly Cham, 33, from Bootle, says the incident has left her unable to sleep with worry.
articles.body:
A single mum-of-two said she was "disgusted" after watching CCTV of an arson attacker setting fire to her home.

Holly Cham, 33, from Bootle, in Merseyside, was away with her children when - in an incident caught on her security cameras - a stranger appeared to emerge from her garage, coming back into view as a fire took hold.

A 31-year-old man was arrested on suspicion of arson with intent to endanger life following a fire on 24 August, Merseyside Police said.

He was released on conditional bail pending further enquiries, the force said.

The footage shows a man appearing from the back of the property and walking away from the garage. Moments later, light shines on the walls of the house as a fire begins to take hold.

The man can then be seen walking along the street and knocking on neighbours' doors before returning to Holly's home and knocking on the front door.

Holly's boyfriend, who was inside the house at the time, answers the door to the man and moves his car off the drive in front of the house.

Holly said her boyfriend had been in the property at the time, looking after the house while she was away with her children.

"I was disgusted," Holly said. "My boyfriend could have lost his life.

"Our neighbourhood is terrified, with neighbours taking turns to keep watch through the night because nobody feels safe.

"The garage has no roof, windows are broken, the house is smoke damaged.

Holly said the incident has left her unable to work.

"While I have a boyfriend but I am a single parent," she explained.

"I run a small business from home but all my stock and equipment have been destroyed.

"I now have to rebuild my business from zero, while losing my only source of income at the same time."

Holly said her boyfriend had been sleeping as the fire took hold, and was woken by a stranger ringing the doorbell.

"He opened the bedroom door and saw smoke coming out coming in from the bathroom window," Holly said.

Holly said her boyfriend called the fire service as soon as he got out of the house.

"They turned up and tried to put the fire out in the garage," she said. "They went in the house and the fire already spread to inside.

"It's broken two windows - I think due to the intense heat.

"Inside the house there's no electricity and my work area and the bathroom is all smoke damaged."

Holly has since moved in with her parents with her six-year-old and her 11-year-old, but she said the upheaval has been a strain for her son Ethan, who has autism.

"Losing his home, belongings and routines has been incredibly difficult for him," Holly said.

"I am grateful that I can stay at my mum's for now but we need to be back in our own place.

"The children are back at school now and it is quite a distance away.

"I'm trying to stay strong for the children but behind closed doors I'm struggling with sleepless nights worrying."

articles.title: Emmy-nominated casting director to rush from wedding to awards
articles.summary: Matt Lander has been nominated for an Emmy for the casting of the drama, All Her Fault.
articles.body:
A casting director from Kidderminster is facing a race against the clock to get from his sister's wedding in Worcester, to the Emmy awards in Los Angeles.

Matt Lander, who left his hometown aged 18 to pursue a career in the US, has been nominated for an Emmy for the casting of the drama miniseries, All Her Fault.

Before he heads back to the US, Lander will be helping his sister, Emma, celebrate her wedding on Saturday.

He plans to leave the celebrations early on Sunday morning, taking a 04:00 BST car to London before catching an 08:00 flight from Heathrow to LA. If all goes to plan he will arrive about two hours before the awards begin.

"Family is everything to me. My sister, this is her first marriage. I really want to be there for her," he said.

He also plans to support his dad, who has dementia and may be unable to fulfil some of the traditional roles expected of a father of the bride.

Lander's sister said she was "absolutely proud" of her brother, describing him as "a fundamental part of the family".

"He flew in last November and spent three days trudging the Midlands to help me find my dream dress, and he even bought that for me," she said.

Brenda Lines, who was Lander's teacher at King Charles I School in Kidderminster, said she was not surprised by his success.

She remembers him as a popular and articulate pupil who was keen to get involved in school life.

"He was driven to be successful and that sort of made him stand out in the crowd," she said. "You knew when you met him that he was going to go places."

Lines said he was always interested in other people, a quality she believes suits his career as a casting director.

"Having the role he has in America is probably quite fitting," she said.

She added that his Emmy nomination was a source of pride for his hometown.

"News like this puts Kidderminster on the map."

Despite the Hollywood lifestyle, Lander said returning to Kidderminster was "really grounding".

"When you grow up here it's some of the most formative years you have," he said.

"I've always had a little bit of imposter syndrome, so when people say congratulations, when people say well done, in my head I'm always feeling like I need to be a step further along."

He said he moved to the US because he wanted to "do something different, experience something new", rather than because of a specific ambition to work in Hollywood.

After studying at an American college, he took various jobs in the industry before finding his way into casting.

He said the job required an "encyclopaedic memory for actors" and a "good sense of people".

All Her Fault has seven Emmy nominations including Lander's, which is for outstanding casting for a limited or anthology series or movie. Another series he worked on, Margo's Got Money Troubles, has eight nominations.

articles.title: Berkshire's Roseanna Brown on her 'amazing' experience on Pressure film set
articles.summary: The actress and singer talks of her famous costars and the "freeing" feeling acting has given her.
articles.body:
"I was in a room full of these amazing actors - it was the most amazing, amazing experience," says Roseanna Brown about her starring role in the latest Hollywood drama, Pressure.

The British-Irish actress and singer, who grew up in Windsor, Berkshire, plays the lead operator in US president Dwight Eisenhower's team in the film - a World War Two drama about the tough choices made in the 72 hours before D-Day.

Cast alongside stars including Brendan Fraser, Andrew Scott and Damien Lewis, it is her biggest role to date, having previously portrayed a Slytherin student in the Harry Potter series and Fandral's Wench in Thor: The Dark World.

Ahead of the film's release in UK cinemas on 9 September, Brown shares how much she learned from the filming and her dreams about future roles.

Brown says she auditioned for the film in 2024 but did not find out what role she had been chosen for until she arrived on set.

"I headed up the entire scene, nobody else spoke," she says.

"I am the first person to receive the information if D-Day was a success or not.

"Surprisingly, even though we know what happened, it was still really stressful to have that situation - even watching it in the cinema, it was still very edge of your seat."

Scott, who is best known for his roles in the hit BBC series Sherlock and the James Bond film Spectre, plays British meteorologist James Stagg , while Academy Award winning actor Fraser portrays Eisenhower.

Brown says she has taken away lessons such as the value in taking chances.

She recalls watching Fraser do the same take where he "responded differently every time", alternating between "an overwhelming amount of emotion" and other times where he "kept his composure".

"I was like, 'oh my gosh, we are all make-believing together while also knowing what the story is and how our characters should be'."

Brown also remembers Lewis, who is known for his roles in Homeland and Band of Brothers, was "really lovely" to her and said hello every morning.

She also says it was "very nice to see the Andrew Scott who wasn't playing James Stagg".

She talks of acting a phone call scene with him and thinking after each cut, "I'm really doing this with Andrew Scott".

Brown says later he praised her for "an absolutely fantastic job" and provided her with specific feedback.

"It's nice to just give space to those people who have quite complex characters to play," she says.

"Damien, for example, very different on set, he'd go into character and out of character, whereas other people very much would stay in."

She says having watched the cast "bounce off each other" had been "amazing to be a part of and learn from".

Pressure was released in the US on 29 May and Brown, who lives mostly in Los Angeles, says she thinks it would have "a different type of appeal" in the UK.

Brown says she now looks forward to landing her dream role and would "love" to star in a Game of Thrones prequel or in the Fourth Wing TV adaptation .

She says she loves historical dramas and fantasy, with her first feature film appearance having been in the Harry Potter series.

But she would also "adore to be the voice of a Disney princess or a Disney character".

As the former front-woman of sibling band The Rua, she has achieved chart success in the UK and the United States, and says she would like to simultaneously develop her acting alongside her music career.

"It's a very different creative feeling where I'm not myself and that is just so freeing," she adds.

articles.title: Lindsay Clancy murder trial has divided US on whether she's victim or criminal
articles.summary: Some say the case shed light on the mental health struggles of mothers, while others argue it's no excuse for murder.
articles.body:
Warning: This story contains distressing details and discussion of attempted suicide

Jodi Fournier spent 15 days at the courthouse - sitting, listening and waiting. It was a personal duty, she felt, to show support for Lindsay Clancy, the Massachusetts mother charged with murdering her three children.

Katelyn Kazmirci, from North Carolina, convinced her mother to make a detour to the courthouse in Plymouth on their way to a family funeral, intrigued by the case she had followed on TikTok.

All around them, dozens of women wearing pink rallied in support of Clancy. Not everyone felt the same and across the country, on social media and at dinner tables, Americans have been debating the case with passion.

For nearly seven weeks, the trial transfixed and divided the nation on whether Clancy was a victim or a criminal who deserved to be behind bars.

The 36-year-old nurse's defence team argued she had been suffering from postpartum psychosis when she strangled her young children and so could not be held criminally responsible. The prosecution alleged the killings were intentional and calculated.

The judge declared a mistrial on Friday after jurors - who had heard the testimony of dozens of witnesses and deliberated for 40 hours - failed to come to a uninanimous decision.

What happens next after Lindsay Clancy mistrial?

Their inability to agree mirrored the wider discourse around the trial - one that trial attendee Maryanne Drysdale, 65, saw play out within her own family.

She and her 28-year-old daughter believe Clancy needs mental health treatment, not prison, while her three adult sons, who have children of similar age to Clancy's, completely disagree.

"It's black and white for them, [Clancy] killed the kids and that's that," she said. "I brought these kids up - how can we think so differently about this?"

Fournier believes Clancy was wronged by the US health system and felt compelled, as a woman and a mother, to show up for a case that has given a spotlight to postpartum struggles.

"It only takes one person to change the narrative," she said. "This is a global issue. This isn't just Massachusetts-small-town. This is... women everywhere."

Clancy claims she experienced hallucinations and delusions before strangling her three children - five-year-old Cora, Dawson, three, and Callan, who was eight months old - and then jumping from a second-floor window, leaving her paralysed.

The court heard testimony from more than 10 expert witnesses on Clancy's mental and postpartum health during the trial.

But some of them seemed to dispute the defence's claim that postpartum psychosis - a rare post-childbirth condition characterised by mania and depression - precluded Clancy from criminal liability.

Jennifer Tufts, who treated Clancy during more than a dozen sessions over five months, testified that she had not shown signs of psychosis.

Psychiatrist Avram Mack later testified that the American Psychiatric Association did not recognise postpartum psychosis as a diagnosis.

Lindsay Clancy's trial puts postpartum psychosis in the spotlight

Mistrial declared in Lindsay Clancy murder case, after jury deadlocks

These declarations only deepened staunch opinions for many - on both sides.

Texas mother-of-four Nicole Russell, who followed the trial remotely, noted the prosecution's presentation of how much medical care and support Clancy had received - from doctors, her husband, nanny and family - calling it "way more help" than most mothers receive.

Clancy's struggles were said to have begun following the birth of her youngest child. She repeatedly sought care, visiting a hospital emergency room, different medical professionals and even calling a suicide hotline.

Many observers took that as evidence that Clancy had been proactive and done everything within her power to heal but had been failed by the system, prompting sympathy from some.

Melissa Merrill had been treated at the same hospital as Clancy after the birth of her son.

"I see myself in her, as a mum who had suicidal ideation," she told the BBC outside the Plymouth courthouse.

Throughout the weeks of emotional testimony, Clancy, who uses a wheelchair, could be seen crying, holding her attorney's hand and making agonised utterances in court as sometimes harrowing details were shared.

After one of the trial days, Merrill rushed to Clancy's defence attorney outside the court and gave him a pink envelope holding a message of support and hope for his client, believing Clancy was a "sad, defeated woman".

But other parents, like Texas mother Russell, railed against "toxic empathy", insisting Clancy was "not a martyr or a symbol for tired mums".

"Lindsay Clancy cannot be the poster child of what difficult motherhood looks like, because millions of mothers give birth to children and endure all kinds of hardship, and they do not hurt their children," Russell argued.

The discourse around the Clancy trial was prominent on social media, with many users being hard-pressed to find a platform where the case was not being mentioned, if not being subject to myriad conspiracy theories.

Clancy's mother, sister and former husband all testified to her deteriorating mental state in the run-up to the murders, but her ex Patrick Clancy was singled out online for wild vitriol and cover-up accusations.

There were claims that he was to blame for the murders, despite his wife never denying killing their children, nor that she had been the only adult at home at the time. This thrust him into the limelight, with tabloids snapping photos of him travelling and with his new wife.

His lawyers issued a statement to CNN in August calling the facts "indisputable".

"Patrick Clancy has suffered an unspeakable and unimaginable loss," they said. "Unfortunately, the tragedy Patrick has experienced has been compounded by patently false, defamatory and injurious public statements."

The case became a flashpoint for gender discussion, too, with opinions often divided along gender lines.

Father-of-three Vincenzo Vazquez, who followed the trial from Illinois, believes gender has a lot to do with Clancy's treatment, doubting that the public would show similar sympathy if a father were on trial for the same charges.

"Whatever someone is dealing with, I don't think there's ever an appropriate time or an excuse or a justification to, you know, kill children of your own, or kill any children," he said.

He said he felt "very sad and a little disgusted to see how many people are rallying behind her", adding: "I think people should be out there rallying for justice for the children. They're three beautiful kids that had a future in front of them."

The decision to declare a mistrial after seven days of deadlocked jury deliberations has left the status of the case - and Clancy's future - unclear. A hearing at the end of the month could establish whether prosecutors will move ahead with second trial or attempt to reach a plea deal.

For now, the debates elsewhere will no doubt continue.

articles.title: ‘Will be compelled to launch large-scale agitation’: Sonam Wangchuk ahead of Ladakh talks with Centre
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: Ladakh-based activist Sonam Wangchuk on Saturday said the Leh Apex Body (LAB) would be compelled to launch a “very large-scale agitation” i.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Ladakh-based activist Sonam Wangchuk on Saturday said the Leh Apex Body (LAB) would be compelled to launch a “very large-scale agitation” if the Union government fails to make “concrete” progress on the group’s key demands.“If stepmotherly treatment is meted out to Ladakh and the people living along the borders, then we will be compelled to launch a very large-scale agitation after September 9,” PTI quoted him as saying. He was referring to the date when an LAB sub-committee is scheduled to meet Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) officials in Delhi to press for its demands.Wangchuk further announced that the outfit's proposed march from Kargil to Leh, scheduled to begin on September 10, had been postponed in view of the MHA talks. However, he warned the march would be revived if the talks fail to produce a “satisfactory” outcome.“We have collectively decided to postpone the 'padyatra' for the time being. We will once again appeal to people from across India to come forward in support of Ladakh, in support of the environment, and in support of the people of Ladakh who remain steadfast on the country's borders,” he stated.He added that the LAB is observing September as “Martyrs' Month” in memory of those killed, injured and jailed last year. The activist was referring to the violence in Leh, the Union territory's capital, on September 24 last year, during which four civilians were killed, allegedly in police firing. Wangchuk himself was detained under the stringent National Security Act and released six months later, in March this year.Wangchuk, who emerged as the face of the recent student protests in Delhi and sat on a hunger strike for more than 20 days, also said the LAB expects the Centre to bring a detailed draft on the proposed Ladakh assembly, including its powers and rights, to the September 9 meeting.The outfit has been demanding legislation for Ladakh at the Union territory level, safeguards under Article 371, withdrawal of cases filed after the September 24 violence last year, compensation for victims and publication of the inquiry commission report. articles.title: At least five killed in Sudan’s South Kordofan in attack by rebel group
articles.summary: Sudan Doctors Network says SPLM-N forces shelled residential areas in the town of Dilling.
articles.body:
Sudanese rebel group SPLM-N has been accused of carrying out artillery attacks in residential areas, resulting in at least five deaths and multiple injuries.

The Sudan Doctors Network has called on the international community to intervene and pressure the SPLM-N to cease attacks against civilians, citing violations of international humanitarian law.

Recent violence in South Kordofan province, including attacks on the Otoro tribe, has added to the ethnic tensions in Sudan's wider civil war, despite a ceasefire initiative last month.

At least five people, including a child, have been killed and several others injured after a Sudanese rebel group attacked residential areas in the South Kordofan province, according to a medical organisation.

The Sudan Doctors Network, in a statement on Friday, accused the Sudan People's Liberation Movement-North (SPLM-N) of carrying out the artillery attack in the town of Dilling.

The organisation said the heavy bombardment of civilian areas was a clear violation of international humanitarian law, resulting in civilian casualties and further worsening an already dire humanitarian situation.

"The Sudan Doctors Network calls on the international community to take immediate action to end these violations and exert meaningful pressure on the leadership of the SPLM-N (al-Hilu Faction) to cease attacks against civilians and residential areas," it said.

The SPLM-N is a breakaway faction of the SPLM, the governing party of neighbouring South Sudan. Its leader, Abdel Aziz al-Hilu, has aligned his fighters with the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and joined ranks with the RSF-led parallel government in Sudan.

In a separate statement issued just hours earlier, the medical group said SPLM-N forces attacked the areas of Debi and Luweri near the town of Kauda on Thursday, killing more than 21 people, including women and children.

The network said those attacks specifically targeted the Otoro tribe, a minority group in the Nuba Mountains.

The killings follow clashes earlier this year driven by land disputes, adding another layer of ethnic friction to the country's wider civil war between the Sudanese army and the RSF.

The recent fighting came despite a ceasefire initiative backed by the RSF last month. Al-Hilu did not commit to the agreement, and his forces launched attacks on at least 10 Otoro villages, displacing thousands of civilians between August 20 and 26.

The escalation coincides with broader warnings from a United Nations-backed independent fact-finding mission, which reported on Thursday that foreign involvement, including external supply networks, foreign personnel, and military drones, is driving the conflict and worsening violence against civilians nationwide.

Since fighting between the Sudanese military and the RSF broke out in April 2023, the war has killed tens of thousands of people, displaced approximately 13 million, and pushed parts of the country into famine.

According to the World Health Organization, nearly 34 million people, about two-thirds of Sudan's population, now require urgent humanitarian assistance.

articles.title: Have scientists discovered a dark matter particle?
articles.summary: Dark matter is an invisible substance that is said to bind the universe; scientists may have found new signs of it.
articles.body:
Deep beneath the Black Hills of South Dakota, US, in an old gold mine, a tank of liquid xenon has been used to produce an unusual particle reaction that may be a link to “dark matter”.

Scientists conducting an experiment there say they have found a single “unexplained particle interaction” that resembles a dark matter particle, though researchers have not called this a confirmed detection.

“Dark matter” and “dark energy” are substances whose presence humans have detected, but have yet to actually observe. This is the closest scientists have come to possibly uncovering the universe’s most elusive form of matter.

Dark matter is an invisible substance that is believed to make up roughly 27 percent of all matter in the universe. Similarly, dark energy, thought to make up 68 percent of everything in the universe, is an invisible force that pushes galaxies apart and speeds up the expansion of the universe.

Ordinary matter, which is everything we can see and touch, accounts for only 5 percent of everything that exists.

Scientists found proof that this unseen matter exists in the universe by observing its gravitational pull, which affects how galaxies spin and how light bends around large clusters of it.

What it is made of, and what it looks like, has remained a mystery to scientists since its discovery nearly a century ago, as it cannot be detected directly because it does not reflect light or electromagnetic radiation.

The first clue to the existence of dark matter was discovered in the 1930s, when Swiss astronomer Fritz Zwicky noticed that the galaxies in the Coma Cluster were moving too fast for the cluster’s visible mass to hold them in place, suggesting something else had to be applying gravity. Similar observations were made over the following decades – all signs pointing to the presence of invisible matter, scientists say.

On Sunday, NASA, the US space agency, announced that it was launching a $4bn project, the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope , which will investigate both dark matter and dark energy.

What have scientists found in the latest experiment?

Scientists say they have found a single unexplained particle interaction that resembles a dark matter particle, though they said this is not the same as directly detecting dark matter itself.

The LUX-ZEPLIN (LZ) experiment was run by an international team of 250 scientists and engineers from 38 institutions. At its centre is an underground tank at the Sanford Underground Research Facility (SURF) in the state of South Dakota, in the United States, which holds ultra-pure liquid xenon, surrounded by hundreds of light sensors.

The theory that the experiment was testing is this: if a hypothetical dark matter particle called a WIMP (weakly interacting massive particle) reacts with the nucleus of a xenon atom, it would produce two flashes of light at a specific energy level.

After reviewing 220 days of data collected between March 2023 and April 2024, the LZ team discovered one such event on June 16, 2023.

Sam Eriksen, the lead of the study and a senior research associate at the University of Bristol, presented the findings on Tuesday at the 2026 TeV Particle Astrophysics conference in Japan.

“We understand our detectors and the backgrounds so well,” Eriksen explained in a press release , “that even a single outstanding event, like the one we found, is important”.

Rick Gaitskell, the LZ spokesperson and a physicist at Brown University, said scientists “don’t want to get ahead” of themselves.

“We are not claiming to have seen dark matter,” he added.

Physicists are calling this the most compelling signal LZ has produced so far, and it could be a signpost to the first real evidence of a particle that physics as we currently understand it has not been able to explain.

Theresa Fruth, a physicist at the University of Sydney who also worked on the study, told ABC News that the event is exciting because it has been re-tested several times and has held up. “This event just won’t go away even after many, many checks.”

articles.title: Winston Churchill bought Chartwell as his family home in 1922; 104 years later, visitors can still explore about 80 acres of grounds
articles.summary: US News: Discover Chartwell, Winston Churchill's stunning property in Kent, open for exploration today with beautiful gardens, lakes, and a rich history.
articles.body: In September 1922, Winston Churchill acquired Chartwell, a red-brick farmhouse on about 80 acres (often cited as 82) in the Kent Weald, some 30 miles south of London. Mainly Museums notes that Churchill's purchase came at a personal and professional low point: the year before, in August 1921, his family had mourned the death of his two-year-old daughter, Marigold, and within weeks of completing the sale he would lose his Dundee parliamentary seat in the November 1922 general election. Chartwell went on to serve as his family home for the next four decades, a period the National Trust confirms in its own account of the property.An undistinguished farmhouse with a view over the Weald It is not the architecture that convinced Churchill to buy Chartwell. He bought a farmhouse that had tile-hung gables and small and dark windows, one that was largely in a dilapidated condition in the latter half of the nineteenth century. It is the sight of the Weald from the garden side of Chartwell that appealed to him. The Historic Environment Record of Kent County Council, under the official entry for Chartwell Garden, mentions how the location is at the head of a valley, with slopes leading south to distant views of the Kentish landscape and plain of River Eden.Philip Tilden's alterations, 1922 to 1924 To turn the farmhouse into a comfortable family home, Churchill engaged architect Philip Tilden, who worked on the property from 1922 to 1924. According to the Historic Environment Record maintained by Kent County Council, Tilden's alterations included adding an eastward wing, a stepped gable on the south front, and simplifying the west elevation.Financial strain nearly cost Churchill his homeIn the decades that followed, Chartwell proved to be far more than a simple retreat: it became an expensive property to maintain. Churchill faced repeated pressure to sell it, most seriously after the Second World War, when his finances were again under strain. In the words of the International Churchill Society, the property continued to weigh on his finances until a group of his friends and admirers, led by Lord Camrose, bought it in 1946.Churchill passed away in January 1965, after Chartwell had been his home, on and off, for nearly four decades, a stretch that included a serious stroke he suffered in 1953 while serving his second term as prime minister, an episode both the National Trust and the International Churchill Society recount in their histories of the house. Clementine relinquished her claim to the property soon afterward, and on 22 June 1966 the Trust opened the estate to the public, as detailed in the National Trust's own account of Chartwell's history. Garden designer Lanning Roper then advised on the grounds from 1965 to 1980, and Historic England's register entry for Chartwell notes that his work, most concentrated between 1965 and 1968, shaped much of the garden's present-day planting and layout, building on the structural features Churchill had already built himself, including the lakes and the kitchen garden walls.80 acres open to visitors More than a century after Churchill signed the purchase papers, 104 years on from 1922, Chartwell remains open as a National Trust property, as the International Churchill Society's own visitor page confirms. Visitors can explore about 80 acres of grounds, including the hillside gardens the Churchills created, the lakes Churchill built, the walled kitchen garden he helped construct, and an orchard surrounded by wildflower meadow. The interiors still hold items Churchill left behind, such as books and personal memorabilia, along with the largest collection of his paintings, exhibited in the studio he used.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Disruption at Port of Dover as masked men hold protest
articles.summary: Protesters, all dressed in black and with their faces covered, are heard chanting "stop the boats".
articles.body:
There is major disruption at the Port of Dover due to a large group of masked men holding a demonstration.

Kent Police said it was aware of a demonstration currently taking place at the ferry terminal and was "engaging with protesters".

Traffic was initially stopped from going in and out of the port but P&O Ferries said access had been restored via the A2. Road access remains restricted via the A20.

Paul King, Reform UK councillor for Dover West, said he had been told the demonstration was a "stop the boats protest", while images from the scene appear to show hundreds of protesters, all dressed in black and wearing face coverings.

Police are marching protesters towards Dover Priory railway station. The demonstrators have been chanting: "Stop the boats".

P&O said it would get passengers on to the next available sailing if they missed their scheduled crossing.

Ferry operator DFDS said it was aware of the "current traffic disruption" and would accommodate passengers on the next departure once they arrived.

Traffic is stopped in both directions on the A20, between the A256 York Street and the A2 Jubilee Way in Dover, according to National Highways.

It is reporting three miles (4.8km) of congestion on the A20 and a further mile of tailbacks on the M20.

Dover and Deal MP Mike Tapp told the BBC the incident was causing "absolutely awful disruption" for residents.

"My understanding is, a number of individuals have travelled to the area, wearing black, wearing balaclavas, and have blocked a number of roads leading into the port area," he said.

Tapp added on Facebook: "I am fed up with idiots coming to Dover to cause disruption.

"I bet if you asked any one of those 'protesters' they wouldn't know small boat crossing are down by 40% and we are working hard to fix the mess."

Kent Police has not yet commented on who is behind the protest.

Remco van Schellen arrived from the Netherlands at about 08:00 BST but when "we wanted to leave the ferry terminal with the car, we couldn't go any further".

"There were people blocking the roads, the roundabout, just outside of the ferry terminal in Dover," he said.

"There were people in black clothing, their faces masked, so we couldn't see who they were."

Chris Vinson, leader of the Conservative group on Dover District Council, said: "Overnight, clearly what appears to be several hundred masked men, wearing black clothing and balaclavas, seem to have coordinated and loaded into rental vans and then descended on roads leading in and out of Dover."

He said the protest appears to be "illegal migration-related" but added that demonstrators do not appear to have placards or banners.

People who worked night shifts at the port have been "prevented from leaving for fears for their safety", Vinson added.

Port of Dover said the "ongoing public order incident" was affecting traffic at the port and town.

In a statement, it added: "We are in contact with Kent Police to understand the situation.

"This situation is impacting our local community and our customers, so of course we are hoping for a swift resolution."

Dover is the UK's busiest international ferry and passenger port, dealing with more than nine million passengers by road and two million freight vehicles in 2025, according to the port's website.

articles.title: UAE pardons Egyptian dissident-poet al-Qaradawi facing 10 years in prison
articles.summary: Egyptian activist Abdul Rahman al-Qaradawi was held due to an arrest warrant by the Arab Interior Ministers Council.
articles.body:
Egyptian opposition activist and poet Abdul Rahman al-Qaradawi has been pardoned ⁠by United Arab Emirates (UAE) President Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan (MBZ), according to state media.

Al-Qaradawi was arrested in Lebanon in December 2024 and extradited to the UAE in January 2025, facing charges of “engaging in activities ‌that ⁠aim to stir and undermine public security”.

The UAE’s state news agency WAM said on Friday that the country’s president issued a pardon for al-Qaradawi, days after he was sentenced by the Abu Dhabi Federal Court of Appeal’s Cybercrime Division on August 27 to 10 years in prison and fined him 200,000 dirhams ($55,000).

It is not known if Qaradawi has been released but WAM reported on Friday that “the necessary procedures have been taken to implement the presidential pardon”.

Al-Qaradawi is the son of Yusuf al-Qaradawi , one of the Sunni Muslim world’s most influential religious scholars, who championed the 2011 Arab Spring uprisings, and drew the ire of leaders in Egypt and some Gulf states.

His family warned in a statement in January 2025 that Lebanon would be endangering his life if it extradited him to any country that demands him.

Rights groups and ⁠UN experts had called for al-Qaradawi’s release, saying he ⁠had been arrested merely for ⁠exercising his right to free speech.

articles.title: A giant US landmark is going dark this September; the surprising reason has everything to do with millions of migrating birds
articles.summary: US News: An iconic American landmark that has been a part of history for more than half a century will be going dark this month in a bid to save lives. The Gat.
articles.body: An iconic American landmark that has been a part of history for more than half a century will be going dark this month in a bid to save lives. The Gateway Arch, which has triumphantly bent over St Louis, Missouri, will now bow to nature. Throughout the month of September, the lights on this Midwestern marvel will be turned off as millions of migratory birds begin their journey south, reported the NY Post.Every evening, the arch's exterior lights will be turned off to reduce the risk of disorienting the birds, as the brightness can cause them to veer into buildings or stray from the correct migration route. St Louis and its resplendent Arch sit critically on one of North America's busiest Avian superhighways, the Mississippi Flyway. According to data from the National Park Service, roughly 40% of the nation's migratory waterfowl rely on this path throughout the year, with many birds travelling under the cover of darkness, making city lights a major hazard.Since 2002, the Gateway Arch has gone dark in both May and September to support the spring and autumn migrations, when more than 300 species of birds pass through the St Louis area. Come October and past the peak of the autumn migration period, the lights will return to their normal schedule.Beyond the big arch lights, the Audubon Society has offered tips on how humans living along the migration path can assist their avian friends this season. These measures include keeping cats indoors and away from songbirds who are passing through. The organisation urges folks to shut off outdoor lights to avoid disorienting the winged. Clear glass is a silent killer for birds, which easily mistake reflective windows for open sky or trees. The Audubon Society advises using decals, paint, or glass markers to disrupt the surface and make the barrier visible.To prevent the spread of disease among migratory birds, the Audubon Society underscores the importance of regularly cleaning bird feeders.Last year, a record number of migrating birds were killed by flying into NYC’s iconic skyline. At least 1,250 warblers, flickers, and other species were lured to their deaths in 2025 during their annual fall pilgrimage, smashing the 2024 record that logged the bloodiest year yet.This comes as the world’s birdlife is already on the brink. A 2019 study by Cornell University in Ithaca found that approximately three billion birds have died off since 1970. The Audubon Society has warned that 389 North American bird species will become extinct within the next half-century. This could have major ramifications worldwide. Roughly 5%of plants rely on birds to pollinate them, meaning that die-offs could cause food production to plummet, thereby disrupting global ecosystems. On an economic level, dwindling bird numbers can impact the production of cash crops such as coffee and chocolate or pharmaceutical precursors.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: A Nigerian engineer built his first model house with 14,800 sand-filled plastic bottles; the experiment later grew into 15 houses, including a five-bedroom duplex
articles.summary: Rest of World News: What if thousands of discarded plastic bottles could become part of a house instead of ending up in gutters or landfills? In Kaduna, Nigerian engineer.
articles.body: What if thousands of discarded plastic bottles could become part of a house instead of ending up in gutters or landfills? In Kaduna, Nigerian engineer Yahaya Ahmed has spent more than a decade exploring that possibility. His first model house used 14,800 plastic bottles filled with sand, an experiment that eventually grew into a broader construction initiative. In an interview with PUNCH, Ahmed, director of the Developmental Association of Renewable Energies, explained how he learned the technique, built the first model and went on to construct as many as 15 houses. Among the projects he described were a three-bedroom house in Ibadan and a five-bedroom duplex in Abuja. He also discussed the method’s claimed benefits, including lower construction costs, insulation and the potential to put discarded plastic bottles to practical use.From waste to wallsAhmed learned the construction technique in Germany from the person he said invented it. He later worked with non-governmental organisations to bring the method to Nigeria, where they organised training before beginning to collect plastic bottles from places such as gutters and farms. The first model was built around 2012 or 2013. At the time, collecting bottles was relatively easy because large numbers were simply discarded. Ahmed and his team worked with unemployed young people who were encouraged to gather the bottles, turning the collection process into a source of temporary work. The project gradually attracted attention, leading to training programmes and construction projects in different parts of Nigeria.How the houses are builtThe process starts with collecting plastic bottles and filling them with sand. The number required depends on the size and type of structure being constructed. According to Ahmed, the bottles are filled manually, making this the most difficult and time-consuming stage of the process. The sand-filled bottles are then incorporated into the walls, while a mixture of laterite and sharp sand is used during construction. The method still uses conventional construction elements where necessary. Ahmed explained that cement can be used for the foundation, depending on the soil, and later for plastering. Doors, windows and interior fittings are also added after the main structure has been completed.Fifteen houses builtWhat began as a single demonstration project eventually expanded into a series of structures. Ahmed said his organisation has constructed up to 15 houses, with projects in Kaduna, Kano, Port Harcourt and other locations. One of the larger examples is a complete three-bedroom house in Ibadan, which is now used as an office and living space. In Abuja, the team constructed a five-bedroom duplex, showing that the technique is not limited to small, single-storey buildings.The idea has also attracted interest outside Nigeria. Ahmed described an invitation from a traditional ruler in Ghana who had seen the projects on YouTube. His team subsequently spent about four and a half months training 15 people in a village near Kumasi.Turning bottles into buildingsThe technique is closely linked to Ahmed’s interest in reducing plastic waste. He pointed to discarded bottles that can clog drainage systems and contribute to flooding, particularly because plastic does not easily decay. Rather than processing the bottles into another product, the construction method keeps them in the building itself. Ahmed describes this as upcycling, because the bottles become part of a long-term structure. He also said the method can make use of suitable sand or clay excavated from a building’s foundation. Instead of discarding the material, it can be sieved and used to fill the bottles.Claimed benefitsCost is one of the major advantages Ahmed associates with the method. He said bottle construction can cost at least half as much as conventional sand- or clay-based construction, depending partly on the availability and cost of the bottles and other materials. He also highlighted the insulating properties of the sand-filled walls, noting that the buildings can remain cooler during Nigeria’s hot seasons and warmer during colder periods, potentially reducing the need for air conditioning. Ahmed further claimed that the structures can remain intact for 200 to 250 years and described them as bullet-resistant, according to the interview with PUNCH.Challenges remainDespite the projects, the approach faces several obstacles. Ahmed identified limited government support, difficulties obtaining construction permits, funding shortages and a lack of public awareness as some of the biggest challenges. The availability of plastic bottles has also changed. As recycling has become more common, bottles that were once freely collected are increasingly gathered and sold by scavengers. Ahmed said they can still be purchased, although this has changed how his team obtains its supplies. For now, sand-filled plastic bottles remain an alternative construction approach rather than a mainstream replacement for conventional building materials. But what started with a single model house has developed into a much larger experiment, with up to 15 houses and other structures built across Nigeria, and the possibility of turning one of the country's most persistent waste materials into part of its built environment.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Pentagon polygraphs dozens of US military staff over media leaks
articles.summary: About 50 officers on the US Joint Staff were interrogated over reports detailing depleted weapons stockpiles, NYT says.
articles.body:
United States investigators have subjected about 50 members of the US military’s Joint Staff to lie detector tests following a series of unauthorised media leaks, according to a report by The New York Times (NYT).

The inquiry focused on whether civilian and military personnel leaked classified details to reporters, particularly concerning dwindling US ammunition reserves , the newspaper reported on Friday.

The polygraph examinations took place last month after news outlets published several reports highlighting severe drops in key weapons supplies, including long-range missiles and Patriot air defence interceptors. US officials had pushed back on these reports, insisting their weapons stockpiles were more than sufficient.

In a statement to the NYT, Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell declined to address internal administrative or investigative actions directly, but emphasised that the department takes leaks of national security information “extremely seriously and investigates accordingly”.

“Securing classified information is critical to ensuring the security of the United States and of our troops deployed around the world,” Parnell added.

The Joint Staff, which consists of between 1,500 and 2,000 military and civilian staff, plays a key role in coordinating operational strategy, policy and war planning with combat commands globally.

Sources familiar with the inquiry told the NYT that the aggressive push was designed not only to identify the individuals behind the disclosures, but also to deter potential future leakers.

Legal and military experts say the scale of the investigation is unprecedented, as the top ranks of the US armed forces have never undergone widespread polygraph testing in modern history.

The move follows widespread reporting on how active military operations involving Iran have severely strained US weapon reserves, causing internal debates over the broader direction of the conflict.

US President Donald Trump has repeatedly pushed officials to crack down on unauthorised disclosures. In addition to calling for strict enforcement, Trump has publicly branded critical media coverage regarding munition shortages and the administration’s handling of the conflict in Iran as “ treasonous ”.

The persistent leaks have deepened an atmosphere of deep distrust inside the Pentagon, which current and former officials attribute to the management style of Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth .

Operating alongside a tight circle of close aides, Hegseth has ousted or blocked the promotions of at least 80 generals, admirals and senior officials during his tenure, the report said.

The Pentagon has launched multiple leak probes in response to media coverage of Hegseth’s leadership, even as he faced criticism for sharing sensitive operational details in a Signal group chat.

The internal tensions escalated further last month when the Defence Department fired the top editor and publisher of Stars and Stripes, an independent, government-funded military news publication.

Staff members said the move was direct retaliation for stories detailing deteriorating conditions on board the aircraft carrier USS Abraham Lincoln .

Despite the mounting friction, Trump has backed Hegseth, publicly praising his performance as “fantastic”.

articles.title: Mansour Abbas is betting on a Zionist to make Palestinian votes count
articles.summary: By allying with Segalovich in the Israeli vote, Abbas is hoping for greater acceptance in Israeli coalition politics.
articles.body:
When Raam leader Mansour Abbas appeared alongside former Yesh Atid lawmaker Yoav Segalovich this week and announced that Segalovich would run second on the party’s electoral slate, much of the immediate attention went to the obvious novelty: An Israeli Jewish politician, openly Zionist and a former police major-general, running near the top of the list of a conservative Islamist Arab party. That combination is unusual, and it was meant to look unusual.

Jewish participation in political lists representing Palestinian citizens of Israel is not, in itself, unprecedented. Hadash was built around a Jewish-Arab political tradition and has for decades included Jewish candidates and lawmakers. Ofer Cassif sits in the Knesset today as one of its most outspoken Jewish members. What is distinctive about the Abbas-Segalovich arrangement is not that a Jew is running with an Arab list. It is the kind of Jewish political voice Abbas has chosen to place there: a Zionist former senior police commander whose political biography sits comfortably inside the Israeli mainstream, not outside it.

Segalovich is joining Raam’s slate, not Raam itself, and the difference is easy to miss if one stops at the photograph. According to the arrangement, he will join the electoral list and parliamentary faction but will not become a member of the party. Raam’s constitution and internal decision-making structure will not change. Segalovich is also expected to retain the freedom to vote independently on questions where the ideological distance is obvious, including religion and state, security and LGBTQ rights. Abbas is not converting Raam into a Zionist party and Segalovich is not becoming an Islamist. They are testing whether two political identities that remain quite far apart can inhabit the same electoral vehicle.

I am not convinced that the main purpose of the move is electoral, at least not in the simple sense of adding more votes. Segalovich may bring some. An August Channel 13 poll suggested that a slate including him could perform somewhat better than Raam has in other surveys, and he retains unusual credibility among Arab local leaders because of his work on organised crime while serving as deputy public security minister in coalition governments led by Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid.

In that period he became one of the few senior Jewish officials associated in Arab public memory not only with promises about crime, but with a governmental programme that actually tried to confront it. That helps Abbas now, when criminal violence remains one of the most immediate concerns of Palestinian citizens of Israel. The arithmetic still looks secondary. What Abbas is trying to change is the political value of the seats he expects to win.

Since breaking with the Joint List and entering the Bennett-Lapid coalition in 2021, Abbas has pursued a fairly consistent experiment. His argument, sometimes stated directly and sometimes only through practice, is that Palestinian citizens of Israel have accumulated representation without converting enough of it into governing power.

Arab parties could win ten, thirteen or fifteen seats and still be treated as politically untouchable when coalitions were formed. He tried to break that wall by making Raam available for coalition politics, including with parties whose positions on the Palestinian question were very far from his own. For a short period it worked, then it didn’t.

The government collapsed, Benjamin Netanyahu returned to power, October 7 arrived and the war that followed eroded the legitimacy Abbas had labouriously built for Arab participation in a governing coalition. Jewish opposition parties that desperately need Arab seats to reach a majority still hesitate to say openly that they would govern with Raam. Avigdor Liberman, who sat in the same government with Abbas in 2021, has already said Raam cannot be a coalition partner this time. Netanyahu has gone back to one of his most effective electoral weapons: warning Jewish voters that his opponents will depend on Arab parties to govern.

Segalovich’s place as number two on the list answers that problem more than it answers a shortage of ballots, because the obstacle facing Abbas was never only how many seats Raam might win, but whether those seats would be treated as usable once the counting was over. Jewish opposition parties may need Arab mandates and still refuse to say, in public, that they would govern with them; Netanyahu’s campaign has long fed on that hesitation and Liberman’s rejection of Raam as a partner shows how quickly the old taboo returned after October 7.

A Zionist former police commander standing immediately behind Abbas does not dissolve the ideological objections to the party, yet it makes the simpler charge – that Raam stands outside legitimate Israeli politics – harder to repeat without looking past the man placed in the second slot. He is not only a candidate. He is a certificate of political usability, a way of saying that Arab votes already cast should count towards government rather than remain representation without power. That may be worth more to Abbas after October 7 than the number of Jewish voters Segalovich can actually persuade to put a Raam ballot in the box.

Abbas has again resisted returning to a full Arab Joint List for the same reason. Hadash, Taal and Balad have rebuilt a reduced version of that alliance and left the door open to Raam, but the two projects are no longer travelling in the same direction. The Joint List is trying to maximise collective Arab representation and keep a recognisably Palestinian political address. Abbas is trying to maximise the ability of Arab representation to enter the machinery of government. The aims can overlap. They are not the same. The Joint List has already criticised him for choosing Segalovich rather than rejoining the Arab alliance, and reports before the announcement indicated it was willing to press Raam to return – without Segalovich.

Palestinian politics inside Israel has carried this tension for a long time, longer than one campaign cycle. Should an Arab party first represent the collective political identity of Palestinian citizens, even at the price of remaining outside government? Or should it accept ideological compromise, perhaps a great deal of it, in order to gain access to budgets, ministries and actual decision-making? Abbas has chosen the second route more clearly than any major Arab leader before him. Segalovich takes the experiment one step further. Until now, Abbas argued that an Arab party could cooperate with Zionist parties. He is now saying, in effect, that a Zionist politician can sit inside an Arab-led parliamentary list without either side pretending their ideological differences have disappeared.

Israeli politics has spent decades demanding that Arab politicians prove they are acceptable partners while rarely making the opposite demand of Jewish parties: that they demonstrate a willingness to share political space with Palestinian citizens as equals. Putting Segalovich second on Raam’s list turns that equation around, at least symbolically. The Jewish partner is no longer inviting the Arab into his coalition. He is entering an Arab-led list.

The price is harder to ignore. The more Raam defines its success through its acceptability to Zionist coalition partners, the greater the temptation to push the Palestinian national question further outside its political programme. Segalovich has been explicit that he remains Zionist and Jewish in his political worldview.

Raam has been equally explicit that it is not asking him to become something else. The honesty is better than a fake ideological unity, but it also lays the bargain out in the open. Abbas gains a partner who can help normalise Raam inside Israeli coalition politics. Segalovich joins a slate led by a party whose strategy increasingly emphasises civil integration, crime, budgets and practical governance while leaving the deepest questions of Palestinian national rights somewhere more distant.

The move will not look the same to every part of the electorate. To some Palestinian voters it may demonstrate maturity: politics is about delivering results, not guarding ideological purity from the opposition benches. To others it will look like another stage in transforming Palestinian political power into a tool whose value is measured by how little discomfort it causes the Zionist mainstream. Neither reading is empty. Asking whether Segalovich will bring Raam another seat or two is therefore a smaller question than the one Abbas is actually placing on the table.

He wants the argument after the election to be less about whether Jewish parties are allowed to rely on Arab votes and more about what they are prepared to offer for them. Segalovich is there to make that conversation easier for Jewish politicians. Whether the same move makes Abbas’s argument easier to defend among Palestinian citizens is a separate problem, and he knows it.

That is not simply coexistence. It is a political transaction, and perhaps a very calculated one. The test will not be how many Jewish voters follow Segalovich into Raam on election day. It will come afterwards, when Jewish opposition leaders still have to decide whether they can say publicly what they struggle to say now: that a government supported by Palestinian citizens and their political representatives is no less legitimate because of it.

If Abbas succeeds at that, Segalovich may bring Raam very few additional votes and still prove one of its most consequential candidates. The thing Abbas is really trying to increase is not Raam’s vote share. It is the political worth of an Arab vote after it has already been cast.

articles.title: 'When were casteist slurs used?' Swatantra supporters protest at police station
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: Several people gathered near the Sansad Marg Police Station on Saturday, protesting against the detention of Swatantra Bharadwaj for allege.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Several people gathered near the Sansad Marg Police Station on Saturday, protesting against the detention of Swatantra Bharadwaj for allegedly assaulting Sanjay Kumar, the father of a teenage student activist, during a July 20 protest in the national capital.One of Bharadwaj's supporters, Daksh Choudhary, said they would also file a counter-complaint against the father of the minor protester and warned the authorities to investigate the matter impartially."We are giving a warning that if the matter is not investigated impartially, and if a case is not registered against the victim's father, whom we have come to file a complaint against this morning, then they can use the pressure of a crowd by gathering people. They can also mobilise a crowd whenever they want," he said.Choudhary also denied allegations that Bharadwaj used caste-based slurs against the student protester or her father."Where were caste-based slurs used? Now you are talking about the Constitution, so tell me this: under the Constitution, if you are abusing someone using caste-based slurs, only then does the SC/ST Act apply. Show me a video! Just show me the video in which he used caste-based slurs," he added.This comes a day after the 22-year-old was arrested from Bulandshahr in Uttar Pradesh on Saturday and sent to 1-day remand after Delhi Police assured CJP protesters that he would be arrested within 72 hours in connection with the alleged assault on Sanjay Kumar, the father of a teenage student activist, during the July 20 protest in the national capital.His detention came after a clip from an interview went viral in which Bharadwaj is heard claiming that he had "cracked the skull" of Kumar, leaving him with an injury that required 60 stitches, and yet managed to avoid being jailed.On Thursday, a day before he was detained, Bharadwaj posted a screenshot showing his name among the trends on X, captioning it, "Love you all Virodhi".Bharadwaj also posted a photograph of himself on Instagram displaying a 'kada' on his wrist with the caption "Feel the power!", an apparent reference to Delhi Police's statement that Kumar was hurt by a 'kada' and "not by any weapon".His Facebook page also carries photographs of him at the Red Fort on August 15, with hashtags such as "#sanatanihero" and "#gaurakshak". In another post, he displayed an invitation issued in his name by the Ministry of Defence for this year's Independence Day ceremony.He had similarly posted photographs of invitations issued to him for the swearing-in ceremony of the Narendra Modi government on June 9, 2024.There are also photographs of Bharadwaj with political leaders, including Bihar Chief Minister Samrat Choudhary, Delhi minister Kapil Mishra and Union minister Chirag Paswan.However, there is no evidence to establish that the political leaders named by Bharadwaj intervened on his behalf in the case.Police officials said several teams were subsequently deployed to trace Bharadwaj. He allegedly fled Naithla village on a motorcycle towards Khurja before a police team could apprehend him there. He was wearing a helmet, apparently in an attempt to conceal his identity.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Netanyahu reached army HQ 2 hours after October 7 attack began: Report
articles.summary: Middle East News: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu may have taken at least two hours to leave his home in Caesarea and reach the IDF’s Kirya military headquart.
articles.body: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu may have taken at least two hours to leave his home in Caesarea and reach the IDF’s Kirya military headquarters in Tel Aviv after Hamas-led terrorists began invading Israel on October 7, 2023, according to a report.The development comes as Israel prepares to hold its next general election on October 27, following the completion of a full four-year parliamentary term under Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s government.The report, aired by Israeli television and cited by The Times of Israel, has raised questions over the prime minister’s movements in the crucial opening hours of the Hamas-led attack, as terrorists were overrunning communities along Israel’s Gaza border.Earlier this week, Netanyahu’s office released what it said were minutes from his schedule on October 7. The records showed that Netanyahu was alerted to the invasion at 6:29 am but did not leave his home until 7:30 am, with his office attributing the delay to preparations for his convoy.According to the released minutes, Netanyahu arrived at the Kirya at 8 am. However, the document also noted that Shin Bet records put his arrival at 8:22 am.Channel 12, however, reported that unpublished minutes from Netanyahu’s diary placed his arrival at 9 am. The broadcaster also quoted a “credible source” as saying the prime minister did not arrive until 9:30 am.If accurate, the report would mean Netanyahu may not have left Caesarea until around 8:30 or 9 am, more than two hours after he was first alerted to the invasion.Netanyahu, Israel’s longest-serving prime minister, has led the country through three years of war.The report also said Netanyahu did not contact his security chiefs after being woken by his military secretary at 6:29 am and did not speak to them until he reached the Kirya.That account contrasts with Netanyahu’s statement earlier this week that, had security chiefs awakened him during the night to brief him on signs of a possible Hamas attack, he would have “immediately” mobilized the IDF and the Air Force.Netanyahu’s first situational assessment at the Kirya was not held until 9:55 am, according to the minutes released by his office. About an hour later, he released a video declaring: “we are at war.”Channel 12 also reported that then-defence minister Yoav Gallant reached the Kirya at 7:30 am, an hour after being alerted. Gallant’s home was around 80 kilometres from the headquarters, while Netanyahu’s Caesarea residence was about 20 kilometres closer.The revelations have renewed calls for a state commission of inquiry. “Precisely on account of these three hours we must establish a state commission of inquiry,” the October Council said.Netanyahu has opposed such a commission. A state commission of inquiry would have broad powers to investigate the events of October 7, including who knew what, who issued instructions and why the government response unfolded as it didCatch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Sheffield teen 'excited' to attend prestigious theatre school
articles.summary: Evie Bradford will attend Lane Theatre Arts - Victoria Beckham is counted among its famous alumni.
articles.body:
"I can't tell you the feeling of walking out of the door after my audition - I just knew that this is where I want to be for the next three years."

For 18-year-old dancer Evie Bradford, the start of the academic year marks the culmination of hours in the studio, and years of rehearsals and competitions.

The teen from Frecheville, Sheffield will soon be treading the boards and honing her craft at Laine Theatre Arts school in Surrey.

The well-known performing arts institution boasts famous alumni including Victoria Beckham, Warwick Davies and West End star Ruthie Henshall.

Evie jokes she's been dancing "since birth", adding: "I was on stage in my mum's belly. Honestly, I've never looked back and thought, this is not what I want to do."

A love for the arts runs in the family - Evie's mum and dad work for Manor Operatic Society as a choreographer and director respectively.

As a former student of Wakefield's CAPA College and a competitor at showcases, including Miss Dance of Great Britain, the teen is no stranger to performing under pressure.

With places on the three-year programme at Laine Theatre Arts school limited, Evie had to demonstrate she could sing, act and dance.

She explains: "I went to my audition and gave it my all because really, what have you got to lose?

"I was stressing so much because I did loads of different auditions, but Laine, as soon as you walk through the doors, you just know that it's the one."

She describes herself as "feeling extremely lucky" to land one of only a handful of coveted spots, alongside one of her best friends.

"I don't know a lot of people around me that have done any of this," she says.

"I feel like I'm quite fresh to it all."

Evie has already packed up her belongings and moved into her new home down south, ready for her new course to begin.

"I'm petrified, but also it's the start of a new beginning," she says.

"It's the start of my life really, because it's what I want to do in the future."

For the moment her focus is firmly on her studies, according to her.

"So [I'm] just going to take whatever comes my way in the next three years.

"I'm excited to make new friends and be with everybody that wants to do the same thing as me, every single day."
