articles.title: Trump signs order to remove endangered species status for grey wolves
articles.summary: The US president says the move will help ranchers, but conservationists say it could derail efforts to recover populations.
articles.body:
Donald Trump has signed an executive order to remove endangered species protection for the grey wolf and a subspecies, the Mexican wolf.

The US president's decision could pave the way for pastoral farmers to kill the canines to protect their livestock. His order said ranchers played a "vital role" in the food supply chain and American cultural heritage.

But conservation groups have criticised the move, saying it could derail long-term efforts to recover the endangered wolf populations.

There were 319 Mexican wolves in the wild in the US in 2025, up from just four when they were reintroduced in 1998, US Fish and Wildlife Service (FWS) figures show.

Meanwhile, there are roughly 18,000 grey wolves across the US, though they are still considered endangered as most of their habitat has been destroyed by humans.

An attempt to de-list them at a federal level in 2022 became tied up in litigation, and some campaigners have indicated they intend to do the same of the US Department of Interior acts on Trump's order.

The executive order does not give ranchers immediate license to shoot wolves preying on livestock, but instead gives Interior Secretary Doug Burgum 90 days to determine whether the grey and Mexican wolf populations had recovered enough to warrant being taken off the endangered species list.

Noting that US livestock herds were at a 75-year low while demand for beef had risen by 10% in the past decade, the order added: "More can and should be done to support this critical industry."

However, environmental groups pointed to studies that suggested wolf attacks on livestock were rare and had little impact on ranchers' income.

"This is a huge distraction to placate a handful of ranchers and make them believe that wolves are a greater threat than President Trump's own policies," said Greta Anderson, deputy director of Western Watersheds Project, which works to conserve wildlife in western US states.

The Wolf Conservation Center noted that ranchers were entitled to up to 100% compensation for any livestock losses caused by wolves under the current system, with individual states providing funding for programmes to deter attacks.

"The Mexican grey wolf is not recovered simply because the population has grown," said Claire Musser, executive director of the Grand Canyon Wolf Recovery Project. "Weakening federal protections now would put decades of recovery work at risk."

The executive order comes as the Trump administration is seeking to lower record-high beef prices for consumers, driven by drought and an outbreak of parasites in US beef stocks.

Ranchers have been frustrated by Trump's decision to loosen restrictions on beef imports to address price rises, putting pressure on their already tight margins.

The US government launched a campaign to systematically exterminate wolves towards the end of the 19th Century. This, along with farmers and landowners trapping and killing wolves, pushed them to the brink of eradication.

Ranchers still view them as a nuisance, which tackling lethally constitutes a federal crime.

articles.title: Unlike Gloria Steinem, I was a tomboy before I knew I was a feminist
articles.summary: “The truth will set you free, but first it will piss you off.”― Gloria SteinemGloria Steinem, feminist, activist and writer, who died Thursday, at the.
articles.body: “The truth will set you free, but first it will piss you off.”― Gloria SteinemGloria Steinem, feminist, activist and writer, who died Thursday, at the age of 92, had once said she became a feminist little late in life, somewhere in her mid 30s, and said she regretted the fact that she “joined the movement so late in my life”. That got me thinking, when did I realize I was a feminist? For that matter, when did you? Because the word “feminism” draws extreme reactions from people. At least, in my experience. I have an equal number of women friends who are feminists, as the number who always make it a point to declare they are not.Once a top Bollywood actress during a casual conversation had told me the same. “Oh, I’m not a feminist. There’s no need in this day and age.” This was about 15 years ago. And it got me thinking… when did I realize I was a feminist? What does it mean to be a feminist? Do we all have to be feminists? Women and men? For people in the 20s, still navigating life, the answers would probably vary. Or, maybe, in the age of social media, everyone asks themselves whether or not they are feminists. Because let’s be honest, our perceptions of ourselves and the world are largely influenced by the reality around us. And for each one of us, it’s different.Steinem, throughout her life, had worked towards bringing women—from different socio-economic classes to different races and circumstances—to fight for themselves. Because she understood what women, all over the world, sometimes understand a little late. Feminism is not a fad. It’s not a fancy word. It is a life-long battle. Some, small and quiet. Some, big and loud. Sometimes, it’s personal. Sometimes, it’s political. But as Steinem, and many other feminist trailblazers have said: “The personal is the political”.Steinem did not view the fight for women’s rights as a battle to gain power over men. Instead, she saw it as an effort to restore full dignity, freedom, and choice to half of the human race. She defined a feminist as “anyone who recognizes the equality and full humanity of women and men”. Her core goal was simple: to create a world where every individual enjoys equal opportunity without bias, stereotyping, or forced social expectations.Why the word "feminism" feels so personalPerhaps that is why the word “feminist” can feel so personal, even when we are talking about something as universal as equality. I suspect many women discover their feminism not through books or political movements, but through small, almost forgettable moments that suddenly refuse to be forgotten.It could be the first time a girl is told not to stay out late because “good girls” do not come home after a certain hour, while her brother is allowed to return whenever he pleases. It could be being told that ambition is attractive in a man but somehow intimidating in a woman. It could be discovering that a woman’s anger is labelled aggression, her confidence, arrogance, her independence, selfishness, while the same qualities in a man are often celebrated as leadership.For me, the realization did not arrive as a dramatic revelation. It came gradually, through observation, conversations, friendships, work and simply growing older. You begin to notice the little negotiations women are expected to make every day: how loudly they speak, how they dress, how much they earn, whether they marry, when they have children, how much they work, how much they sacrifice. And then you begin to notice something else: how often women are expected to explain choices that men are simply allowed to make.Perhaps feminism begins precisely there, with that questioning. Why should this be different for her? Why is this acceptable for him but not for her? Who decided that this was the natural order of things?And perhaps being a feminist does not mean having all the answers. It means being willing to ask those questions, even when the answers make us uncomfortable. It means recognising that equality cannot be conditional on whether we personally have experienced discrimination. It means understanding that another woman’s freedom does not diminish our own, and that the choices we make for ourselves should not become rules imposed on everyone else.Steinem spent decades asking uncomfortable questions, including questions about power, privilege, sexuality, work, marriage, motherhood and the invisible systems that determine whose voices are heard. Her legacy lies not merely in the causes she championed, but in the permission she gave generations of women to question the roles they had inherited.So perhaps the more interesting question is not whether we call ourselves feminists. Perhaps it is whether, when confronted with inequality, we are willing to recognise it, question it and, when possible, change it. Some of us may discover our feminism in our twenties. Some may stumble upon it in our thirties, forties or fifties.I’ll add another slice of my own life here. During my school years, I was what this world calls a ‘tomboy’. Largely, this means, one doesn’t have overtly feminine traits. And there was this phase, somewhere around our teenage years, where there is almost a sense of pride declaring to the world that we are tomboys, not silly girls. For some women, it is a personality trait. But for most, it’s “cool”. Because it has always been cool for women to have some boyish traits for boys to accept women as one of their tribe.It was much later in life that I thought of this again. And then some more. Largely because by that time going through life, it had become pretty clear to me that men were largely human beings, but women… were just women. So, I turned the statement “I’m a tomboy” on its head. Who were the boys around me, in my teenage years, who proudly proclaimed: “I have a feminine side in me, and I’m proud of it.” Or, "Masculinity isn’t the only definition of being a boy or man.” Because, really, it isn’t. I could find none.It’s quite insidious actually, the way society's unspoken patriarchal views are carried forward. By men and women. By boys and girls. But what Steinem had shown through her journalism, activism, books and articles is that it’s all okay. Because everyone has to realize and see and feel the inequality on their own to realize why feminism matters.The existential rage is quiet, but it's thereLet me ask a simple question, when you look around your office, especially leadership positions, how many cool cabins are women sitting in? How many times have you been made to feel inadequate not fulfilling what is considered a woman’s job or responsibility? How many times have you walked on the road without considering what to wear for your own safety? How many catcalls did it take for you to finally be silent and do nothing about it, because it is exhausting to scream and shout, and “create a scene” every day? How many days go by without all of us reading horrific articles of another woman burned to death because of dowry?This is where feminism becomes less about a word and more about a way of seeing. Because once you begin to notice these things, it becomes difficult to unsee them. You see them in the jokes that are allowed to pass because “that’s just how men talk”.You see them in meetings where a woman makes a point that nobody notices until a male colleague repeats it. You see them in the expectation that a woman will remember the birthday, organise the dinner, take the child to the doctor, look after an ageing parent and still arrive at work looking as if none of these things required effort. You see them in the strange social approval that comes when a woman is successful but not “too successful”, confident but not “too aggressive”, independent but still sufficiently accommodating.And you see it in the language we use. A man who is assertive is a leader. A woman who is assertive can be difficult. A father who spends time with his children is praised for being involved. A mother who does the same is simply doing her job. A man who prioritises his career is ambitious. A woman who does it is often asked how she is balancing everything.None of these things, individually, may seem like a battle worth fighting. That is precisely how inequality survives. It does not arrive wearing a uniform. It is disguised as a joke, a compliment, a tradition, a piece of advice, an expectation, a raised eyebrow. It tells you, gently at first, what women should be and what they should not be. And because everyone around you appear to accept it, you begin to accept it too.Steinem understood how deeply these ideas could become embedded in us. She once observed, “A pedestal is as much a prison as any small, confined space.” It is such a deceptively simple thought, but it explains so much of what women have historically been offered in place of equality: admiration instead of freedom, protection instead of independence, idealisation instead of agency. Being told that women are special can sometimes be another way of telling them they are different — and therefore subject to different rules.That, perhaps, is the most insidious part of patriarchy. It does not always require men to impose rules on women. Women can become its most efficient carriers, passing down to daughters the same warnings their mothers once gave them: don’t be too loud, don’t be too ambitious, don’t come home too late, don’t dress like that, don’t make him feel insecure, don’t earn too much more than him, don’t make your husband look small, don’t be difficult. Sometimes we call this wisdom. Sometimes we call it culture. Sometimes we call it being practical.Steinem never dictated, she asked questions that cannot be ignored And sometimes it is simply fear, inherited from one generation to the next. This is why Steinem’s work remains so relevant. She did not simply tell women to become stronger. She encouraged them to examine the structures that had taught them what strength was supposed to look like in the first place. She questioned why women had to adapt themselves to a world designed largely around male experiences. She questioned why women had to earn their freedom by proving they were responsible enough, respectable enough, educated enough or successful enough to deserve it.And most importantly, she understood that feminism could not be one-size-fits-all. The woman struggling to survive in a village, the woman fighting for equal pay in a corporate office, the woman raising children alone, the woman choosing not to have children, the woman who wants to be a homemaker, the woman who wants to run a company, the woman who wants to marry, the woman who does not — all of them deserve agency over their own lives.Which brings me back to my teenage self, proudly declaring that I was a tomboy. I had thought I was rejecting the stereotype of the “silly girl”. I did not realise that somewhere beneath that declaration was another, quieter message: being like a boy was somehow a little more valuable. Being tough was cool. Being emotional was not. Being independent was admirable. Being traditionally feminine was something to be slightly embarrassed about.It took me years to understand the absurdity of that equation. These may sound like small things. But lives are made up of small things. And so are inequalities. Steinem understood that. She understood that a revolution does not always begin with a march or a law or a speech. Sometimes, it begins with a woman sitting across from another woman and saying, “You too?”Sometimes, it begins when a daughter questions something her mother accepted. Sometimes, it begins when a son refuses to laugh at a sexist joke. Perhaps that is why another of Steinem’s observations has stayed with me: “The future depends entirely on what each of us does every day; a movement is only people moving.” It takes feminism out of the realm of grand declarations and places it firmly in ordinary life. In what we tolerate, what we challenge, what we teach our children, what we say to our friends and what we choose to remain silent about.Steinem believed she became a feminist late. I suspect many of us do. So the question is not really whether “we have always been feminists”. Perhaps it is when we first became uncomfortable with an inequality we had previously accepted. When did we first ask why? When did we first say, quietly or loudly, that this was not fair? When did we first realise that another woman’s freedom was connected to our own?For me, I think I am still becoming a feminist. Perhaps that is the more honest answer. Maybe that is why Steinem’s words continue to resonate. Feminism was never supposed to be a finished destination. It was always a process of seeing more clearly.She wrote in her 2015 book, My Life on The Road, looking back, “I was angry about the human talent that was lost just because it was born into a female body, and the mediocrity that was rewarded because it was born into a male one."Does that resonate?Looking for trusted parenting advice? articles.title: Mayo: Eoin Doyle, 12, died in collision between car and train
articles.summary: The crash that killed the child happened when a train collided with a car near Ballyhaunis.
articles.body:
A 12-year-old boy who died when a train hit a car near Ballyhaunis in County Mayo has been named locally as Eoin Doyle.

The incident happened at about 20:45 local time on Friday, when the boy and his father were travelling in the car at a user-operated level crossing at Kiltybo.

His father was taken to hospital by ambulance. Gardaí (Irish police) have said that his injuries are not life threatening. All passengers on the train safely disembarked.

Eoin was a sixth-class pupil in Cloonfad National School, and was a member of Ballyhaunis GAA club and Cloonfad United FC.

Ballyhaunis GAA club said Eoin was a "talented young footballer" and a "wonderful young boy who was a great friend and teammate to so many within our club".

Ballyhaunis parish priest Fr Stephen Farragher told Irish broadcaster RTÉ there was an "air of shock and sadness" in the area.

"It's the kind of thing you hope you won't be hearing on the news and you hope it won't be visited on your own community."

Fr Farragher said he was called to the scene, where emergency services were already in attendance.

"I said some prayers with the little boy and spoke to the members of the gardaí, I spoke to members of the family," he said.

Fr Farragher told RTÉ that the boy was coming from underage training at the time that the incident occurred.

"They're a very known, loved family, both families of the young boy's mam and dad are both very well known locally," he said.

In a statement, the principal of Cloonfad National School, Shane Morgan, described the little boy as a "talented artist and athlete, who loved music and a smile was never far from his face".

Gardaí are appealing for witnesses to this incident to come forward.

articles.title: Philippines vice president posts bail after arrest order for alleged threats against president
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — Philippines Vice President Sara Duterte posted bail Saturday after an order was issued for her arrest the previous day on charges that she publicly threatened to arrange the assassination of President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.
articles.body: MANILA, Philippines — Philippines Vice President Sara Duterte posted bail Saturday after an order was issued for her arrest the previous day on charges that she publicly threatened to arrange the assassination of President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. and two other people. Emerging in a black outfit from Quezon City Regional Trial Court in Metro Manila, Duterte consoled her supporters, hugging a woman who was sobbing as supporters chanted “Duterte! Duterte!” The vice president, who has denied the allegations, showed a court order lifting the arrest warrant issued by the court Friday and said her lawyers instructed her to keep a copy on hand. She urged journalists to surround her on the way to her car because she did not feel safe. “If possible please go with me, because I do not feel safe with all these police personnel who are harassing those at my home, harassing me since 2023,” Duterte said. “What does this administration really want to do with me?” Paul Lawrence Lim, one of her attorneys, said court staff took Duterte’s fingerprints and she posted 360,000 pesos bail ($5,740) for three counts of grave threats. After the arrest order was issued Friday, he said Duterte would fight the charges. “She has no intention of evading the law and will continue to exercise all her legal remedies,” he said in a statement. Case based on comments during online news conference The case is seen as part of a high-stakes political showdown pitting Duterte against Marcos. A conviction may permanently disqualify her from holding public office and prohibit her from seeking the presidency in 2028, when Marcos’s six-year term ends. The charges stem from an alleged threat Duterte, 48, made during a 2024 online news conference. She said she would have Marcos, his wife and then-House of Representatives Speaker Martin Romualdez killed by an assassin if she herself was killed as their political disputes escalated. The vice president warned during the event that her threat was not a joke. Duterte later said she was expressing concern for her own safety and not threatening Marcos as the remarks set off a criminal investigation and national security concerns. The House of Representatives, which is dominated by Marcos’ allies, voted overwhelmingly in May to impeach Duterte over allegations of unexplained wealth, misuse of confidential state funds and the online news conference threats. The Philippine Senate, acting as an impeachment court, opened her televised trial in July. Former political partners turned rivals Marcos and Duterte were running mates in the 2022 elections in an alliance that combined two of the country’s most formidable political dynasties. Marcos is the son of former President Ferdinand Marcos Sr., who held the office from the 1960s to the 1980s, including a period of repression and martial law. The vice president is the daughter of former President Rodrigo Duterte, the predecessor to the current President Marcos. Rodrigo Duterte was arrested in 2025 on orders of the International Criminal Court and detained in The Hague, where he is scheduled to face a trial beginning in late November over alleged crimes against humanity connected to a brutal anti-drug crackdown that left thousands of mostly poor suspects dead. He has denied authorizing extrajudicial killings but repeatedly threatened suspects with death while in office. Sara Duterte previously criticized the Marcos administration for surrendering her father to a foreign court, which currently has no jurisdiction over the Philippines. Marcos and Sara Duterte also have contrasting geopolitical leanings. Marcos has expanded defense engagements with the United States, a treaty ally of the Philippines, as his administration stood up to China’s increasingly aggressive actions in the disputed South China Sea. The vice president has come under fire for not condemning China’s assaults, including with the use of powerful water cannons, against Filipino forces and fishermen in the disputed waters.

articles.title: Five EU countries move towards first ‘return hub’ for rejected asylum seekers
articles.summary: Europe News: Five European Union countries have agreed on concrete steps towards establishing a “return hub” in a non-EU country for migrants who do not have legal.
articles.body: Five European Union countries have agreed on concrete steps towards establishing a “return hub” in a non-EU country for migrants who do not have legal residency, as European governments seek to speed up the return of people whose asylum applications have been rejected.Germany, Austria, Greece, Denmark and the Netherlands announced the agreement on Friday after a meeting hosted by Denmark in Copenhagen. The countries said they aim to reach an agreement with a partner country this year, although they did not identify the country being considered.“We want to reach an agreement with third countries this year that will enable the establishment of return hubs,” German interior minister Alexander Dobrindt told reporters in Copenhagen.Danish Immigration and Integration Minister Morten Bodskov said Denmark expected to be ready to send migrants to a return hub by the end of 2027.Greece's migration and asylum minister Thanos Plevris said the goal was to have a hub operational outside the EU by 2027.EU migration rules pave way for centres outside EuropeThe initiative follows changes to EU migration policy. The European Parliament approved an overhaul of migration rules in June that allows member states to establish centres outside the EU and send rejected asylum seekers there instead of returning them directly to their home countries.The five countries said they had agreed on a model for such facilities. The group plans to meet again in Munich, Germany, at the end of September.Bodskov described the move as a transformation of Europe's asylum and migration system. He rejected the suggestion that return hubs would be detention camps.“We are not talking about camps, we are talking about opportunities, for a new chance for irregular migrants who cannot return to their own country today and who have no legal grounds to be in our countries,” he said, according to news agency AP.The ministers said the proposed hubs would operate in accordance with European and international law. The Netherlands' minister of asylum and migration Bart van den Brink said technical talks and missions to potential partner countries would examine human rights conditions and living standards.Rwanda among countries in talksThe five governments have not disclosed which countries could host the facilities. The nations have been negotiating with governments, mainly in Africa, over potential locations.Rwanda confirmed in August that it had begun preliminary discussions with unnamed European countries about potentially hosting asylum seekers who are not allowed to remain elsewhere.Rwandan government spokesperson Yolande Makolo said one idea involved providing a safe place where people could receive medical care, training and rest while their cases were processed.The terms of any potential arrangement, including what partner countries could receive in return for accepting rejected migrants, have not been disclosed.Rights groups raise human rights concernsThe proposed return hubs have drawn criticism from human rights organisations. The Council of Europe said in July that such centres posed “considerable human rights risks”.Council of Europe Commissioner for Human Rights Michael O'Flaherty said that “vague assurances of compliance with human rights law are not enough”.The Danish Refugee Council also criticised the approach. Its secretary general Charlotte Slente said return hubs would deal with only a limited number of returns and could raise concerns over migrants' rights.“Return hubs focus on a small number of returns, they will not stop people from taking even more dangerous routes, and they could violate basic human rights,” she said.The UN Refugee Agency said it had not been approached with details of the proposal and therefore could not comment on the specific arrangements or any potential role for UNHCR.The European ministers said the proposed hubs would be established in line with human rights and international law.Van den Brink said the partner-country discussions would include examining “the human rights situation and the living conditions of the refugees”.The initiative also faces opposition within Europe. articles.title: China silences flood victims to spotlight Xi Jinping's rescue efforts

articles.body: More than a week after a deadly flash flood tore through valleys along the China-Nepal border, the scale of the disaster is becoming clearer, but on the Chinese side, the victims themselves remain largely unseen. Reports indicate that China is exerting extreme pressure to monitor reporting surrounding the disaster.The disaster has killed more than 1,300 people and left more than 5,600 missing across the two countries, according to the latest figures cited in reports. Yet China has released information about the disaster slowly and tightly controlled access to affected areas, offering little public detail about those who died or remain missing.Chinese authorities' death toll update on Friday, raised the number killed in Tibet to 31 and said 531 people remained unaccounted for. An earlier update had put the toll at 21 dead and 541 missing, including 261 foreigners from 23 countries.The information vacuum has drawn attention to China's longstanding restrictions on reporting natural disasters, restrictions that are particularly severe in Tibet, where communications are closely monitored and foreign journalists require special permission to travel.Chinese state media outlets Xinhua and CCTV have been allowed into the affected areas, but their coverage has largely focused on the government's rescue and relief response. Reports have highlighted President Xi Jinping's instructions, rescuers working in difficult conditions and the logistics of delivering aid, rather than identifying victims or giving families a public platform.Human Rights Watch said some Chinese journalists had been instructed not to interview relatives of people killed or missing and to rely only on material provided by Xinhua.The Associated Press said it requested permission to visit the affected areas soon after the disaster but had not been granted access.The restrictions have also extended to social media. Chinese state media circulated details of 10 cases in which people across the country were detained or fined for allegedly spreading rumours about the disaster. Punishments included police detention of between five and 10 days, with some people also fined.One social media post questioned the official death toll, claiming that far more people had been swept away than authorities had reported.Stark contrast to Nepalese coverageThe response stands in stark contrast to neighbouring Nepal, where authorities have provided regular updates on those killed, missing and rescued. The Nepalese army has released footage of helicopter rescues and survivors being pulled from mud-filled hydropower tunnels, while journalists have been able to visit affected sites, rescue camps and burial grounds.The difference was underscored by the rescue of a Chinese national from a hydropower tunnel in Nepal on Saturday, 10 days after the disaster. The man, identified by the army only as Luhaitao, was found alive inside a 225-metre tunnel at the Upper Trishuli-1 Hydropower Project.Video released by the Nepali army showed rescuers giving him medical attention inside a helicopter before taking him to an army hospital. He appeared exhausted and disoriented, with mud and dust covering his clothes and skin.On the Nepalese side, families have also been able to make their own searches public, with some holding symbolic burial rites for relatives whose bodies have not been recovered.On the Chinese side, however, relatives of missing people have had far fewer avenues to seek information publicly. An independent Chinese media outlet operating in exile interviewed families of missing Chinese nationals, including Peng Guangming, a young man working on a Chinese-supported highway project in Nepal. Peng was last in contact with a colleague about 10 minutes before the flood.Another missing Chinese national, He Hongrong, was last seen on the Nepal side carrying a green backpack and waiting to cross into China. Her family has circulated her photograph online in the hope that someone can provide information about her whereabouts.The tight control is especially significant in Tibet, a Chinese autonomous region that has experienced decades of political unrest and government repression. Foreign travel there requires special permission, while restrictions on communications make it difficult for Tibetans to freely share information with people outside China.China has also previously faced criticism for slow-moving disaster reporting. After severe flooding in Guangxi in July, authorities increased the official death toll more than a month later from 39 to 159.The difference in reporting exposes how China lets victims become invisible in order to protect the state machinery.Catch the latest World News and Live updates.
